items.title: Welcome to Non-Deterministic Ramblings
items.text: Welcome to this web site, where I hope to be able to record some slivers of wisdom drawn from many years working in IT. Along the way I have met with people and circumstances, many nice but occasionally some not so pleasant, but from each hopefully I have learned something, and if I record it here I hope that you too may find something of value, if only for any humour.

items.title: "Non-Deterministic"
items.text:
A long, long time ago I studied Computer Science, and while I wasn't very good at the wider mathematics courses, I felt a keen affinity with Discrete Mathemmatics. Part of the discrete maths course concerned itself with Non-Deterministic Finite Automata, or NDFA. By all means follow the links for more information, but in those relatively early days, we studied what is now Automata Theory as a precursor to understanding syntax analysis.

For many years, I joked that for all the time we spent studying NDFA I never had one cross my desk, and I think the probable cause which really defines a lot of my reflections in this blog, are that at the time I studied, we did not have the resources to actually build the range of tools we have now that do use state graphs within them.

More recently I have studied Systems Thinking as a post-graduate abd as part of systems modelling we very much get into Determinism. This is when I think of NDFA and smile to myself, as an NDFA as a state machine could not determine an absolutes state given the input. And so it is with my thinking, in producing this blog my ideas seem to go off in myriad directions, rarely taking teh same path twice from any given starting point.

So please excuse the randomness of the pasts, hopefully they do follow in some sort of logical progression

items.title: "Ramblings"
items.text:
Roughly, I have tried to divide the posts on this into under three broad sections

  • Reflecting - We came, we saw, we experienced, and we would like to help you not to fall into the same traps as maybe we did
  • Thinking - in an area dominated by formal certifications and methods, but latterly a paucity of research finding, we develop heuristics that we think may help explain some of the things we see happening in real-world situations
  • Doing - some words about how I have gone about doing some of the IT things I do

I hope that there is something here that will amuse, maybe promote thoughts of your own, and if it does help in any way then my work here is done.

Expressed Views

Please note that all of the views I express on this site are all my own and do not reflect the views of any of my employers past or present

items.title: Russell
items.text:
Despite attempts using AI to make the photo of me look like some sort of secret agent, my career has spanned well over 40 years in and around computing. Starting at a time when it was called Computing, I have worked in Information Technology aka "IT", battled with the Nexus of Forces, and emerged blinking into the light of Digitalisation. EVen now as I write this during summer 2026, the emergence of AI is changing things once again.

I am certainly old enough now that whenever some bright young thing tries to show me something amazing, I can say "Oh we've been able to do that for years ... Nothing New".

Over that time, I started as a programmer, then moved to Product Management, before spending the last 25 years as variously a Solution Architect, an Enterprise Architect, and latterly focussing on Business Architecture. The piece about Purpose of an IT Architect at ../blog/posts/Whatis.md) is based upon a myriad of conversations arising from this time.

Academically I have a BSc in Computer Science, an MBA, and an MSC in Systems Thinking in Practice. However despite attending many courses, and passing exams, I am very much in favour of praxis as part of my daily practice.

Hopefully this site contains aspects drawn from a wide variety of experiences. At the top of this site you'll find links to ways to contact me.

items.title: Photographs
items.text:
While I infrequently use images to lighten pages, where I do unless specifically tagged all images are my own. When I remember I shoot with a Panasonic Lumix GX7, otherwise photographs have been captured using my iPhone with either the default camera shipped by Apple, or ProCamera when I am able to master the settings and make it work for me.

At the moment I am using Affinity on my laptop as the image editor.

For many years I have used Paint.NET which is an excellent image editor in my opinion, with a superb set of plug-ins. However it is only available for Windows[61]. I am lucky that in my current job I have access to Paint.NET via the organisations software policy.

I have dipped in and out of usingGimp for many years, and the recent set of add-ons to make Gimp present as much like Adobe as it can is, I think, a big boon for the software. Like a lot of users, I find that my 'muscle memory' for Paint.NET afflicts my use of any other image editor hanse my comments about the Adobe style presentation add-ions for Gimp 3.x.

But to bring this page to a close, I feel that the time has come to address my own 'muscle memory' issue and learn a new image editor. At teh moment, Affinity from Canva is getting rave reviews, and it works well. I particularly like that it combines three tools into one - page layout, vector graphics, and image editing all in one application, it reminds me of the (very) old Windows Works package that combined word processing, spreadsheet, and a rudimentary database, and served me well for wrting my MBA siigenments back in the mid-90s. I digress....

items.title: What is the purpose of an Enterprise Architect?
items.text:
The books tell us lots about what an Enterprise Archiect should do, but what is the reality. After over 25 years in teh role, here is my personal veiw

The irony here is that I have been working as an architect in IT for over 25 years, and yet when pushed I still couldn't tell you exactly what an architect in IT actually does, I can tell you from my experiences, but put a group of IT architects in a room together, and I would suggest that getting a consensus would be difficult.

Let me try and explain...
path: What is the purpose of an Enterprise Architect?

items.title: What sort of "Architect"?
items.text: I've seen several attempts to define the types of architecture practice found in IT. All have had a common theme insofar that all were different. Yes, there have been degrees of overlap between formal definitions but the actuality of where "... rubber meets the road ... " shows a much wider diversity amongst definitions.
path: What is the purpose of an Enterprise Architect?

items.title: So who creates these "forma" definitions, and why?
items.text:
I could go back into a history of IT architecture, but maybe I'll reserve that for another post. I could also give a cynical answer that the formal definitions tend to be made by folks who make money by defining them, but that isn't strictly true

It is fair to point to the certification bodies, who make their money from training, examining, and certifying people in architecture disciplines. I can see a form of value for people being able to show that they can learn material and reproduce it in an examination of some sort. To be able to test, you need to define what is to be tested. Different organisations who can make money from this service need to differentiate themselves, hence one source of variation.

But that isn't the only source of these differences. My own experiences working in public sector have been both helped, and hindered, by teh UK Civil Service defining career profiles for different types of architect working in GDAD. As a former manager trying to recruit, this framework helped to provide consistency and a career progression framework. However, as a contributor to developing a framework (in this case defining Business Architect roles), the approach was remarkably insular without considering the delivery a architecture services and practice holistically.
path: What is the purpose of an Enterprise Architect?

items.title: So where did that Architect go to?
items.text: Whilst there is a overwhelming need for architecture skills, the challenge lies in the diversity of the organisations that we all work in.
path: What is the purpose of an Enterprise Architect?

items.title: Is "Bytes, Boards, Boxes?" still applicable in 2026?
items.text:
A university lecture in 1982 provided both a technical framework, and wider life-lessons, but does the lesson stand today?

The complete post continues here.
path: Is "Bytes, Boards, Boxes?" still applicable in 2026?

items.title: Bytes, Boards, Boxes
items.text:
In my final year at university studying computer science, there was one lecture that not only made an impression on me at the time, but in the intervening years has stood the test of time and with reflection has increasingly served as a metaphor for life in general.

Delivered as a 50-minute lecture as part of a module on computer architecture, the content has been a major takeaway from my entire degree. I am not aware of wWhether or not this is still taught now as part of any computing related degree, but in my humble opinion it really ought to be as I believe the context holds as true today as it was in early 1982.
path: Is "Bytes, Boards, Boxes?" still applicable in 2026?

items.title: A 1982 Approach to architecting computer-based solutions
items.text:
1980s context

At the time of the lecture, there was a lot of compute capability available, both in terms of processor power or memory capability. Our ability to interface computers to the real world was also limited.

The key problem being addressed by this lecture was what is the best way to go about building a system, based around computing hardware, to meet a requirement? One example I saw after university was a hardware design for a firm-control computer for use by artillery.

Given the paucity of developed compute solution as we know them today required a framework for architectural decisions making:

Approach Description Pros Cons Bytes Solution design from individual hardware components Can be made very specific to solving need Difficult to debug / Difficult to customise or update to serve a similar requirement Boards Design based upon a combinations of pre-built boards Boards present pre-debugged chunks of functionality, debug only inter-connections / Potential to repurpose for similar requirements Not as specific to a solution, may require trade-offs in requirements matching Boxes Use a complete, working box for the solution Using a completely debugged solution saves development time Solution may need significant compromises to requirements, or software fixes

The key decision point largely came down to how much time did you have to debug the hardware, Tracey Kidder covered this far better than I ever can in his book The Sould of a New Machine covering teh development of a new computer system, a Box from the components, the Bytes.

My Real-World Example

My first job after university was about addressing the problem of how can we capture and store voice messages? The problem needed to solve some interesting dimensions:

  1. We had to link to a digital telephone line serving voice channels, but the silicon device we had planned for was severely delayed
  2. Storage devices had small capacity, and each voice channels was data intensive1
  3. We needed a general compute server to run a real-time operating system and control everything

The answer we came up with at the time turned out not be a clear cut case of one approach, but a hybrid...

  • There was no box solution, so that was out immediately
  • There were some board solutions available: processor boards, memory boards, storage controllers so they presented a shot cut to the control portion
  • The boards were linked using {Intel Multibus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multibus) as a standard interconnect
  • Our plan to use a simple chip for the telephony link had to change to building a board full of chips, and a lot of debugging
  • The research team came up with a compression solution using early DSP ssystem on chip soluions which required their own board ... more hardware debugging
  • All of the above required controlling software
path: Is "Bytes, Boards, Boxes?" still applicable in 2026?

items.title: Technically, has 'Bytes - Boards - Boxes' endured?
items.text:
Many technology changes over the intervening forty years have changed the landscape. One irony is that not long after our work in teh example above, a customisable box solution came available which would have saved some of the time we spent simply getting a set of pre-developed boards working together, but we would still have had the other challenges.

My reflection of the changes amounts to:

  • Bytes: Silicon fabrication technology and techniques has created on-chip capabilities way beyond anything we could have anticipated back in 1982, for example a board full of components for a PC board a few years later is now routinely delivered on one silicon component. Our need to string together so many components has reduced.

    More recently the componentization of chiplets and the ability to combine chiplets on a single silicon die has moved the whole Bytes architecture decisions towards the large manufacturers and chip fabricators, as well as raising the economic factors in these decisions.

  • Boards: The original approach of a standard interconnect bus with boards plugged in has been largey left behind by the increasing capabilities available on a singly silicon component. This in turn has created an architecture for Single Board Computers SBC) cards such as the Raspberry Pi.

However, these SBC products have been developed with defined connectivity, such as the General Purpose I/O (GPIO) standard which supports additional plug-in modules, and some development boards for customised hardware solutions.

  • Boxes: The "siliconisation" of components, such as storage devices has merged the distinction between boards and boxes, witness the Raspberry PI as delivering what would previously be a box solution as a standalone single board|

The decision frameworx still endures, but the decision points have moved.
path: Is "Bytes, Boards, Boxes?" still applicable in 2026?

items.title: Bytes - Baords - Boxes as a Metaphor
items.text:
The main reason that the lecture has stuck with me reflects my experiences in my roles, and life in general. Whenever solving a problem I tend to think of possible solutions, and the impacts in terms of:

"Bytes" What happens if we put together a lot of different parts to solve our problem. What are the integration challenges (for example, what do i need X to tell Y) An example could be putting my own holiday plans together from teh individual parts "Boards" Are there some integrated parts I can hook into. Using my holiday example, what if I use one company for all my travel needs, flights, car hire etc, and then one hotel chain for different parts of the itinerary? "Boxes" Can I get a single solution with everything pre-integrated? A package holiday? A new build house?
path: Is "Bytes, Boards, Boxes?" still applicable in 2026?

items.title: Final Thoughts - Systems Engineering
items.text:
In my practice as an Enterprise Architect, this approach based on Bytes - Boards - Boxes as a metaphor is always part of my toolkit, especially when developing options for stakeholders. In working through teh life-cycle of a project, I can map Bytes - Boards - Boxes metaphor over the Systems ENgineering V Model starting with "Boxes" at teh top level working all teh way down to "Bytes" at the point of the V.

What started as a simple hardware lecture all those years ago has turned into one of the most used tools in the toolbox of my working practice.

  1. Well, 64kbps per channel was deemed very data intensive in the day ↩
